meta.blurb: Why does a person need to wander outdoors with no goal at all? Thoreau's famous essay answers with swamps, sunsets and a daily saunter of four hours. Walk through his ideas and find a calmer, wilder way to spend an afternoon.
meta.bible: Henry David Thoreau: American writer and naturalist of the nineteenth century, born in Concord, Massachusetts, died on 6 May 1862 aged 44 of Tuberculosis. Walking: his essay on the art of walking and the value of wild nature, printed in The Atlantic Monthly in June 1862, soon after his death; it grew out of lectures he gave in the 1850s. Concord: his home town in Massachusetts. Walden Pond: the pond near Concord where he lived in a small cabin for about two years from 1845. Saunter, Sauntering, Saunterer and Saunterers: Thoreau's word for walking slowly and freely with no goal; he gives two stories for where the word comes from, and they are guesses. Holy Land: the Sainte Terre of the old pilgrims, Sainte-Terrer. Wildness: his word for the free, untamed life of nature, which he values highly. Swamp: the wet, dark wood he loves to visit. Pilgrims, Knights. Atlantic: the ocean. Atlantis and Hesperides: legendary western islands of the ancient poets. Lethe: the river of forgetting in Greek myth. Old World and New World. Oregon: then the far west of the country. Romulus and Remus: the founders of Rome in the old tale, said to have been nursed by a she-wolf. Europe, America, Asia, Rome, Latin, Greek. Latin saying quoted by Thoreau: light comes from the East, fruit from the West. Key quotations are real and short: Eastward I go only by force; but westward I go free; and In Wildness is the preservation of the World. Thoreau was a writer and not a doctor; the health remarks are his own opinions. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: calm, curious, a little humorous and very outdoors; Thoreau's own opinions are always marked as his.

B1B2: Henry David Thoreau lived in Concord, Massachusetts, and walked in the countryside almost every day. His essay about walking was printed in 1862, soon after he died.
Thoreau begins by saying that he wants to speak a word for Nature, and for wildness and freedom. He means a freedom much wider than the rules and manners of ordinary society.
Most writers see a person as a member of society, with a town, a job and a set of rules. Thoreau would rather see him as a part of Nature, like a tree or a bird.
Thoreau believes that walking well is an art, and that very few people have the talent for it. In all his life, he says, he has met only one or two who really understood it.

Thoreau gives two stories for where the word saunter comes from, and he likes them both. In the first, wanderers of the old days said they were walking to the Holy Land, and children called them Sainte-Terrers.
The second story says that saunter comes from words meaning without land. A person with no home of his own, Thoreau says, is really at home everywhere, and that is the secret of sauntering.
In a playful passage, Thoreau pictures walkers as a kind of knights, who leave home and go out into the world with no fixed plan. A walk, he says, is a small crusade for the freedom of the spirit.
Thoreau says, in his dramatic way, that you are ready for a real walk only when you have paid your debts and settled your affairs. Then you are free to set out, as if you might never come back.
Thoreau says that he spends at least four hours a day walking through the woods, over the hills and across the fields. For all that time he wants to be completely free from every worldly duty.

Thoreau sees shopkeepers and clerks sitting indoors, day after day, many of them with their legs crossed. He is surprised that they can bear it, and he wonders what it does to their health and spirits.
Thoreau says that he could not keep his health and spirits without several hours outdoors each day. He is only describing his own life, and other people, of course, are different.
Thoreau is alarmed when he has walked a mile into the woods and his mind is still back in the village. Then the body has gone, he says, but the spirit has not arrived.
Thoreau asks a sharp question: what business has he in the woods if he is thinking of something outside the woods? A walker should leave his worries at the edge of the trees.
Thoreau says that roads are made for horses and for men of business. He seldom uses them, because he is in no hurry to reach any shop or station.
Thoreau says that the country within ten miles of his home offers enough walks for a whole life. Even seventy years, he believes, would not be long enough to know it properly.
Thoreau says that even his nearest fields never become quite familiar to him. The light, the weather and his own mood change every day, so each walk shows him something new.
When we walk, Thoreau says, we naturally go to the fields and the woods. He asks what would become of us if we walked only in a garden or a shady public walk.
Thoreau notices that, when he sets out, he is always pulled toward the west, or a little south of west. He does not choose it; some force inside him seems to do it for him.
He compares himself to the needle of a compass, which trembles a little but always points the same way. Some days it swings a few degrees, but it settles between the west and the south-west.
Thoreau writes, “Eastward I go only by force; but westward I go free.” The east feels like the past to him, and the west feels like the future.
Thoreau says that he must walk toward Oregon, then the far west of the country, and not toward Europe. The future, he feels, is that way, because the land there seems larger and fresher.
Thoreau quotes an old Latin saying: light comes from the East, but fruit comes from the West. He likes the saying because people and their ideas have so often moved westward over the centuries.
The ancient poets told of golden islands in the far west, such as the Hesperides and Atlantis. Thoreau likes to imagine that those old dreams were really about the land he lives in.
Thoreau calls the Atlantic a Lethe, which was a river of forgetting in the old Greek stories. Crossing it, he says, gave people the chance to leave the habits and rules of the Old World behind.
With a smile, Thoreau argues that the sky seems higher and the stars seem brighter in America. He hopes that this is a sign of how high the thoughts of its people may one day rise.
Thoreau writes that his hope and his future are not in lawns, farms, towns or cities. They are, he says, in the wet and shaking swamps that nobody has tamed.

When he wants to refresh himself, Thoreau looks for the thickest and darkest wood, which a townsman would call a gloomy swamp. He enters it as a sacred place, where he feels the strength and the marrow of Nature.
Thoreau's best-known sentence is, “In Wildness is the preservation of the World.” By wildness he means the free, untamed energy of Nature, which he thinks that every person and every town needs.
Thoreau remembers the old tale that Romulus and Remus, who founded Rome, were fed by a she-wolf. He takes it as a sign that strong nations draw their strength from something wild.
Thoreau says that in books, too, only the wild really attracts us. A dull book, he thinks, is simply a tame one.
A truly good book, Thoreau says, is as wildly natural and mysterious as a fungus or a lichen. To him, the best writing has grown rather than been built.

Thoreau jokes that politics is only a narrow field, and the narrow road to it is easy to find. If you want to go to the political world, he says, just follow the man who is taking his goods to market.
Thoreau wonders why a nation should not keep wild preserves, where bears and panthers could still live. Such places, he says, would not need any village to be destroyed.
One day in late November, after a cold grey day, Thoreau was walking across a meadow at the start of a small brook. Just before sunset, the sun reached a clear gap on the horizon.

The softest, brightest light fell on the dry grass, the tree trunks and the leaves of the small oaks on the hill. The long shadows stretched across the meadow, as if people were the only specks of dust in the beams.
The air was so warm and calm that nothing was missing to make the meadow a paradise. Thoreau felt that he could never have imagined such light a moment before.
Such an evening is a gift that comes without notice. Thoreau thinks that only a person who is outdoors, and awake to it, will ever see it.
Thoreau writes that life goes together with wildness, and that whatever is most alive is also most wild. Something that is not yet tamed by man, he says, refreshes whoever meets it.
Thoreau lived for about two years in a small cabin at Walden Pond, near Concord, from 1845. He kept a long journal, in which he wrote about the walks he took, the plants he found and the weather.
Thoreau does not ask his readers to live in the wilderness. He only shows how a small daily walk can make a life feel larger.
Thoreau died of tuberculosis in 1862, at the age of 44. His essay on walking was printed that June in a magazine called the Atlantic Monthly.
Thoreau ends his essay by saying that we saunter toward the Holy Land. He means a place that is not on any map, but that we may reach a little more each time we walk.
Thoreau says that one day the sun may shine more brightly than it has ever done before. He hopes that light will come into our minds and hearts as well as onto our fields.
Thoreau imagines that this light will wake us up, and make the whole of our lives bright. In his mind, a walk in the open air is the first step toward being fully awake.
He says that the light will be as warm and calm and golden as it is on a grassy bank in autumn. With this gentle picture, the long essay comes to its end.
Since his death, many writers and campaigners for wild places have quoted Thoreau. His line about wildness is one of the best known in the history of nature writing.
You do not need a mountain or a long journey to take a walk in Thoreau's spirit. A field, a stream or a quiet park near home may be enough.
To walk as Thoreau did, go slowly, leave your worries at the gate, and notice what is around you. Even a short walk can feel long if your mind is really there.

Today, doctors and health bodies commonly recommend regular walking for most adults. Thoreau was a writer, not a doctor, so anyone with health worries should ask a health professional before changing what they do.
This book is general information about Thoreau's ideas on walking, and it is not medical advice. Please take your walk gently, and enjoy every step of it.
C1C2: Henry David Thoreau, a writer who lived in Concord, Massachusetts, spent much of his life on foot, wandering the fields, woods and swamps around his home. In an essay called Walking, printed in 1862 just after his death, he tried to explain why those wanderings mattered so much to him. Let us follow his argument step by step, as he followed the old paths of his own countryside.

Thoreau opens his essay with a plain declaration: he wishes to speak a word for Nature, for absolute freedom and wildness, as against the freedom and culture that are merely civil. By civil freedom he means the kind that laws, votes and good manners can give, which is real but narrow, and which leaves out much of what a person needs. His essay is a long walk away from that narrow ground and out toward open country where nobody is in charge.

Most writers, Thoreau observes, treat a human being as a member of society, a creature of laws, schools and churches, and they seldom look beyond the edge of the village. He would rather start from the open country and see a person as an inhabitant of Nature, one living thing among countless others. Seen from there, he suggests, many of our proud and anxious little affairs begin to look smaller, and the world itself begins to look larger.

Walking, Thoreau insists, is an art, and like any art it asks for a gift that few people are born with. In the course of his whole life he had met only one or two persons who truly understood what it means to take a walk. Most people, he thought, either hurry toward some destination or swallow their exercise like a dose of medicine, and neither kind of person is truly walking.

Thoreau offers two possible sources for the word saunter, though the true origin of the word is not known. In the first, idle wanderers of the Middle Ages went from village to village, saying that they were bound for the Holy Land, until the children began to cry that there goes a Sainte-Terrer. A saunterer, then, would be a person who walks as though on a pilgrimage, with every step counting for something even if nobody knows where it leads.

The second story is that saunter comes from the French sans terre, meaning without land or a settled home, and Thoreau takes the idea in its best possible sense. A person who owns no particular corner of the earth, he argues, is equally at home in every corner of it. That, in his view, is the whole secret of successful sauntering, and it is a secret worth keeping.

In a playful passage, Thoreau pictures walkers as a sort of knighthood, people who leave the comfortable village behind and go out into the world with no fixed plan. He half hopes that such an order might be revived, although its members would travel on foot rather than on horseback. Each walk, in this spirit, becomes a small crusade for the freedom of the mind, undertaken without armour, banners or any enemy.

In his dramatic way, Thoreau says that to be ready for a true walk you must be willing to leave father and mother, wife and children, and to set out as if you might never see them again. You must have paid your debts, made your will and settled all your affairs, so that you are a free person and carry no unfinished business into the woods. Only then, he claims, are you truly ready to take a walk, and not before, however much you may long to leave.

He declares that he cannot do without at least four hours a day, and often more, spent sauntering through the woods and over the hills and fields. Those hours must be absolutely free from worldly engagements, he insists, with no errands to run and no appointments to keep. It is a generous allowance of time, and he does not apologise for it.

Thoreau looks at the shopkeepers and clerks of his village, who sit indoors for most of the day, many of them with their legs crossed, as if legs were made to be sat upon rather than walked upon. He is amazed that they can bear it, and he wonders aloud what such a life must do to a person's health and spirits. To him, a day without the open air is a kind of quiet poverty.

Thoreau confesses that his own health and spirits depend on these hours, and that without them he would slowly wither. He is describing his own case rather than laying down a law for everyone, and he is honest about how odd his habits must look to his neighbours. Whatever one thinks of his arithmetic, the point is that he treats time outdoors as a need and not as a luxury.

Sometimes, Thoreau admits, he walks a mile into the woods and discovers that he has not really arrived, because his thoughts are still busy with the village and its business. The discovery alarms him, for it shows how little of him has actually come along on the walk. A walk, he seems to say, is measured not in miles but in how much of yourself is present for it.

In one of his sharpest questions, Thoreau asks what business he has in the woods at all if he is thinking of something that lies outside the woods. The walker, he suggests, must work to return to his senses, so that he can see, hear and smell what is truly in front of him. That is not easy, but a walk spent in daydreams about work is hardly a walk at all.

Roads, Thoreau remarks, were made for horses and men of business, and he travels on them comparatively little, since he is in no hurry to reach the tavern, the grocery or the railway station at the end. He prefers to cut across the fields, to follow a brook or to push through a hedge, wherever the land and his curiosity lead him. In this way, he feels, the country is not merely something to be passed through but something to be met.

Within a circle of about ten miles around his house, Thoreau tells us, there is more country than a person could properly explore in a lifetime. The walks that an afternoon allows, he says, match the length of a human life, which he puts at about seventy years, and they never quite become familiar. It is a comforting thought for anyone who believes that wonder requires a ticket and a long journey.

Even the nearest meadow, Thoreau finds, never quite becomes familiar, because the light, the season and the walker's own mood are never the same twice. A path trodden a hundred times can still surprise a person who walks it with open eyes. The traveller who needs a new country every week, he implies, may simply be someone who has not yet learned how to look.

When we walk, Thoreau says, we naturally head for the fields and the woods, and he asks what would become of us if we walked only in a garden or a tidy public mall. Tame places have their charm, but they ask little of us and show us little that we have not already seen. The mind, like the body, he thinks, needs ground that is a little rougher than a path.

Setting out from his door in the afternoon, Thoreau finds that he is nearly always drawn toward the west, or a little south of it, toward the open land and the far horizon. He cannot fully explain the pull, and he does not try very hard to resist it. It seems to him that the direction chooses the walker rather than the walker the direction.

He compares his own instinct to a magnetic needle, which trembles and wavers a few degrees from day to day but settles, in the end, on a direction somewhere between west and south-west. The needle, he adds, does not obey his reasoning, and he has learned to trust it with the humility of a navigator trusting a compass. Where it points, he feels, the future lies, and he is content to follow it without asking for proof.

“Eastward I go only by force; but westward I go free,” Thoreau declares, and he means it both as a plain fact about his afternoon walks and as a larger idea about where a free life lies. The east, with its old cities and old habits, stands for the past, while the west stands for the future and the unfinished. He does not claim to be able to prove this, only to feel it every time he sets out.

I must walk toward Oregon, Thoreau says, and not toward Europe, and in his day Oregon meant the far western edge of the continent, where settlers had only just begun to arrive. The land in that direction seemed to him richer, less used up and more full of promise, like a field that no one has yet ploughed too often. Whether or not he was right about the soil, it is clear that he used the west as a picture of hope.

He recalls an old Latin saying, which promises light from the East and fruit from the West, and he takes it as a hint that the harvests lie in the direction of the sunset. Over the centuries, he observes, the great movements of people have run westward, as if following the sun across the sky. The idea is more poetry than proof, but he is clearly delighted that his own pull toward the west keeps such good company.

The ancient poets, Thoreau recalls, placed their fabled islands in the far west, among them the Garden of the Hesperides and the lost land of Atlantis, where the sun went down into the sea. He fancies that those old dreams of a golden land beyond the ocean were a kind of rumour of the continent where he lives. It is a charming thought, and he offers it as a fancy rather than as history.

Thoreau describes the Atlantic as a Lethe, the river of forgetting in Greek myth, and he suggests that in crossing it the settlers had a chance to forget the Old World and its institutions. To a man who loved fresh starts, the ocean looked like a great page being turned. He is well aware, of course, that people carry most of their habits with them wherever they go.

With a smile, Thoreau declares that in this country the heavens appear higher and the stars brighter. He trusts that these facts are a symbol of the height to which the thought, poetry and religion of its people may one day soar. He cannot prove it, of course, and he knows that the same stars shine over every land, yet the wish behind the joke is serious, for wide horizons make for wide minds.

Hope and the future, Thoreau writes, are for him not to be found in lawns and cultivated fields, nor in towns and cities, but in the dark and quaking swamps that no one has drained or tamed. It is an unexpected place to look for hope, and he enjoys the surprise it gives his readers. The swamp, to him, is the part of the world that has not yet been made to do as it is told.

When he wishes to refresh himself, Thoreau looks for the darkest, thickest and most tangled wood, which the townsman would call a dismal swamp, and he walks into it as into a sacred place. There, he feels, lie the strength and the marrow of Nature, in a ground that is still rich because no one has ploughed it away. To a cheerful walker, the very gloom of the place is a kind of shelter.

His most famous sentence in the whole essay is this: “In Wildness is the preservation of the World.” By wildness he does not mean disorder or danger but the free, untamed energy of living things, which he believes a healthy person and a healthy town can never do without. Life, he adds, goes together with wildness, and whatever is most alive is also most wild.

Thoreau recalls the old tale that Romulus and Remus, the founders of Rome, were nursed by a she-wolf, and he thinks that it holds a truth. The founders of great states, he argues, drew their nourishment from some wild source, and an empire that forgets its wildness may be overcome by people who have not forgotten theirs. It is a bold claim, more a poet's than a historian's, but it shows how seriously he took the value of wild places and wild habits.

In literature, Thoreau says, it is only the wild that really attracts us, and he adds, with a grin, that dullness is just another word for tameness. The writers he loves are those whose work has the freshness of the open air, who say what they have actually seen instead of what is expected. A page that has been tidied until nothing surprising is left in it, he feels, is a page that has lost its life.

A truly good book, Thoreau writes, is something as wildly natural and mysterious as a fungus or a lichen, as if it had sprung up out of the ground rather than been planned at a desk. He says this in praise of old and great works, which seem to belong to the world itself and not only to their authors. The best writing, he thinks, grows from the same soil as the swamp and the forest.

Thoreau jokes that politics is only a narrow field, and that the narrow highway running toward it is easy to find, for anyone who wants the political world has only to follow the market-man along the road. He does not say that government is unimportant, only that it is a small part of the great landscape of a human life. To him, a person who spends every hour thinking about it has mistaken one corner of the country for the whole.

Thoreau asks why the nation should not set aside great wild preserves, where no villages need be destroyed and where the bear and the panther may still live, rather than being civilised off the face of the earth. It was a farsighted idea for a man writing in his time, before national parks had become a familiar idea. He wanted the wild to survive not only for the animals' sake but for the sake of the people who need to meet it.

He tells of a remarkable sunset on a day in late November, when he was walking across a meadow at the source of a small brook after a long, cold and grey afternoon. Just before the sun went down, it reached a clear band at the edge of the sky, and the whole scene changed in a moment. Thoreau had set out as an ordinary walker with an ordinary mood, and he was not expecting anything at all.

The softest and brightest light imaginable fell on the dry grass, on the stems of the distant trees and on the leaves of the small oaks upon the hillside. The shadows of the walkers stretched far across the meadow to the east, as though they were the only specks of dust floating in the beams. Every blade and leaf, for a few minutes, seemed to have been dipped in gold.

It was a light, Thoreau says, that he could not have imagined a moment earlier, and the air was so warm and serene that nothing was wanting to make a paradise of that humble meadow. He stood still, since there was nothing better to do than to stand still and receive it. It is the kind of hour that no clerk at a desk can buy, and no schedule can promise.

Such an evening, Thoreau reflects, arrives without warning, like a gift that is left at the door of whoever happens to be outside and awake. A person who sits indoors, thinking about errands, will never know that it came, however many times it comes. This is the best reason he can give for going out each day: the wonderful hours do not keep appointments.

Life, Thoreau claims, goes together with wildness, and whatever is most alive is also the wildest, since a thing not yet subdued to human purposes brings a freshness that the tame cannot. He loves to see a hawk, a deer or a storm cloud for exactly that reason. In such meetings, he says, we are reminded that the world is bigger than our plans for it.

Thoreau lived for about two years, beginning in 1845, in a small cabin that he built at Walden Pond, a short walk from the village of Concord. He kept a long journal of the walks he took, the plants he found and the weather he met, and he was never very far from home, which is part of his point. The wildness he praised was near enough to reach on foot, and anyone with a field, a stream or a patch of woods nearby, he implies, already owns what he is describing.

Thoreau never demands that his readers abandon their homes and settle in the wilderness, and he lived within easy reach of a village and a post office himself. What he offers instead is a modest practice: a daily walk, taken slowly and without a purpose, with the senses wide awake. The gain from it, he believes, is out of all proportion to the time it takes.

Thoreau died of tuberculosis on the sixth of May, 1862, at the age of only 44, and his essay on walking appeared in the Atlantic Monthly in the following month. It grew out of lectures that he had given in the 1850s, and he had been revising it in his last illness. For that reason, it reads in places like a farewell to the open country he had loved.

Near the close of the essay, Thoreau returns to the pilgrims of his first page and says that we saunter toward the Holy Land. It is a place that is not on any map, and one that every walker approaches a little more nearly with each unhurried afternoon. The journey, as always with him, is as important as the arrival, and perhaps more so.

He hopes, he says, that one day the sun will shine more brightly than it has ever done before, and perhaps shine into our minds and hearts, not merely onto our fields and roofs. It is the oldest wish of every thoughtful walker, that the world outside may light up the world within. In his closing sentences, the plain and practical essayist becomes a poet at last, and the walk becomes a wish for the whole world.

Thoreau imagines that this light might fall on the whole of a human life with a great awakening, so that we would suddenly see the world and our days in it as they truly are. Such an awakening, he implies, cannot be ordered up by a schedule or by a book, though a walk may be the best way to prepare for it. The thought is as large as anything in the essay, and it grows quietly out of an ordinary afternoon.

That light, he says in his final line, will be as warm, serene and golden as it is on a grassy bank in autumn, when the long afternoon sun lies low across the fields. It is a quiet picture to end on, for it asks for no great deeds and no special place. All it requires is a person who has gone out for a walk and is willing to stand still when the sun comes through.

Since his death, many writers, walkers and campaigners for wild places have quoted Thoreau, and his line about wildness is among the most familiar in the whole literature of nature. Not everyone agrees with every opinion in the essay, and a modern reader may well smile at some of its claims. Yet its central request, to go out, to look and to be present, is one that readers of every period have felt able to accept.

One lesson that a modern reader may take from Thoreau is that the adventure need not be far away, since a field, a stream or a quiet corner of a park will do as well as a mountain range. What matters is the quality of attention that we bring, and the freedom we allow ourselves from the day's business. The cost is nothing, the equipment is a pair of comfortable shoes, and the reward may be a small, lasting calm.

To walk in Thoreau's manner, set out without a destination, leave your errands and your screens behind, and let the afternoon decide where you go. Notice the birds rising from the hedge, the smell of wet leaves and the way the light changes along the path. Even a short walk, taken in this spirit, can feel longer and fuller than a long one taken in a hurry.

Today, doctors and health organisations commonly recommend regular walking to most adults, and many studies link an active life with better health, although such studies show a link and not a certain cause. Thoreau, however, was a writer and not a doctor, and his four hours a day are one man's opinion rather than a medical rule. Anyone with a health condition, an injury or a worry about exercise should ask a doctor or another health professional before changing what they do.

This book retells Thoreau's essay and offers general information about his ideas, and it is not medical advice, so please speak to a doctor or another health professional about your own needs. Walk gently, within your own limits, and let the open air do what it can for you. When you next step outside, remember his promise: in wildness, and in a good long saunter, there is a little preservation for the world.
